planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly onto thin, gravelly, well-drained soil so winter cold provides the natural stratification needed for spring germination; established plants can also be set out as small transplants in spring.

directions: This wiry, succulent perennial forms a tuft of round, pencil-like leaves rising from a woody rootstock wedged into cracks of thin rock-outcrop soil, including the magnesium-rich serpentine barrens of the Pennsylvania-Maryland Piedmont. In mid to late summer it sends up slender branching stems tipped with small pink, five-petaled flowers that open only in the afternoon and wither by evening, lasting a single day each. Give it the leanest, most mineral soil available and skip supplemental watering once roots are established, since rich garden soil or regular irrigation causes it to rot or flop. It is best suited to a rock garden, gravel bed, or green roof where it will not be shaded out by taller, faster-growing neighbors.

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions into lean, fast-draining soil in early spring; this low mat-forming native tolerates the thin, rocky, mineral-stressed openings typical of serpentine outcrops far better than it tolerates rich, moisture-retentive garden beds.

directions: Field chickweed spreads into a low, gray-green mat of narrow leaves that is smothered each spring in small white flowers with deeply notched petals, giving the appearance of ten petals rather than five. It is one of the few herbaceous groundcovers that persists in the open, rocky gaps of serpentine barrens where competition from taller grasses is limited by poor soil fertility. In cultivation it works well edging a rock garden path or filling gravel between flagstones, and it shears back easily after bloom to keep the mat tidy. Avoid heavy mulch or fertile soil amendments, which encourage rot and let more aggressive plants crowd it out.

subcategory: serpentine and dry barrens annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter the tiny seed on bare, thin soil in fall so it experiences winter cold and germinates as a low rosette; it also self-sows readily once a colony is established in open, disturbed, mineral-poor ground.

directions: This slender annual produces a single upright stem lined with small, rounded, stem-clasping leaves that cup each flower like a tiny collar, hence the common name. Lower flowers along the stem stay closed and self-pollinate, while the upper blooms open into five-pointed violet-blue stars that draw small native bees. It thrives in the thin, open, frequently disturbed soil typical of serpentine barren margins and roadside edges where taller vegetation cannot establish a closed canopy. Let seed drop in place at season's end rather than deadheading, since the colony depends on fresh disturbed ground each year to persist.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, sterile, sun-baked soil after the last frost, since this wiry annual needs exposed mineral ground with little organic matter and cannot compete where other plants have already filled in.

directions: Orangegrass gets its name from the faint citrus scent released when its tiny, scale-like, tightly appressed leaves are crushed, giving the wiry stems a leafless, wire-like look from a distance. Small yellow flowers open along the upper branches through summer, followed by capsules that shed abundant seed into the bare mineral soil the plant depends on. It is among the few herbaceous species that reliably colonizes the barest, most nutrient-starved patches of serpentine and other rock-barren openings, so it is best used in a dedicated gravel or hardpan planting rather than a conventional bed. Resist the urge to fertilize or mulch, since enriched soil quickly lets grasses and taller forbs outcompete it.

planting.note: Set divisions or small transplants into lean, thin, acidic soil in spring; this low, wiry-stemmed runner spreads readily by rooting at the nodes and needs no irrigation once established in rocky or sandy ground.

directions: Dwarf cinquefoil hugs the ground with palmately divided, strawberry-like leaflets and sends out thin, wiry runners that root as they go, quickly knitting together a low mat over thin, rocky soil too poor for most turf grasses. Cheerful five-petaled yellow flowers dot the mat from spring into early summer and continue sporadically through the season. It handles the mineral-stressed, well-drained openings of serpentine barrens and dry Piedmont outcrops better than most lawn alternatives, making it a useful no-mow groundcover for a rock garden edge or gravel path. Once it fills in, simply shear back any overly long runners that stray into neighboring beds.

planting.note: Sow directly onto thin, gravelly, exposed soil in fall so the seed gets the winter chilling it needs to break dormancy, then flowers the following spring from a low basal rosette.

directions: Also known by its older name Arabis lyrata, this short-lived rosette-former wedges itself into cracks and thin soil pockets on rock outcrops, including the serpentine barrens of the Pennsylvania Piedmont, where its deeply lobed leaves hug the ground through winter. In spring, slender stems rise above the rosette carrying small four-petaled white flowers followed by narrow, upright seed pods. It persists by reseeding into open mineral ground rather than living many years in one spot, so leave some bare gravel nearby for new rosettes to establish. Plant it in a scree bed or crevice garden where taller, moisture-loving perennials cannot shade it out.
